description: Building an interactive climate-risk mapping platform for smallholder farmers using NASA Earth observation data (POWER, MODIS NDVI, GPM precipitation). The tool visualizes crop-specific climate threats  drought stress, heat anomalies, flood risk on a per-field level, helping farmers adapt before losses hit. Stack: React, MapLibre GL, Python data pipeline.
summary:
On 18 July 2012, a wheat farmer in Kostanay looked at a green field and saw nothing wrong. Fifty-five days later, Kazakhstan’s wheat harvest came in 49 % below the year before. The signal was already there that morning  in the soil water, in the heat at flowering  but nobody had turned it into a number the farmer could read.

Field Shift does that. It is a map where you click a rainfed wheat field in Northern Kazakhstan and, in under two seconds, get one risk score, the main threat, and the sowing date that holds up in a bad year. No sensors, no login, no forecast - only free NASA data and the textbook physics of a soil-water balance.

We did not ask anyone to trust it. We put a time machine inside: replay any season since 1984 and watch when the warning appears. Replayed on 2012, it raised “high caution” on 18 July. Across 33 years of real harvests the score tracks yield at ρ = −0.63.

The same data covers every rainfed grain belt on Earth.
details:
What it does & how it works. Field Shift is a map of climate risk for rainfed grain in Northern Kazakhstan, read season by season. Click any cropland point - or a back-tested field - and in under two seconds you get one risk score (0-1), the main threat, how the season ranks against that place’s own 40 years, and the sowing date that holds up in a bad year. Click a town, lake or bare ground and it says “not cropland” and points to the nearest field.

The score is physics, not a guess. Since 1984, NASA POWER gives daily temperature, wind, sunlight, humidity and rain; a FAO-56 soil-water balance turns these into water needed vs water received. A second term counts +31 °C days at flowering on already-dry soil - the heat-and-drought mix behind the 2012 collapse. The two become one number, ranked against the field’s own record. SMAP sets the starting soil moisture (2015->; earlier from snowmelt or full profile, stated in-app), SoilGrids the water capacity, SRTM elevation, ESA WorldCover the cropland gate, MODIS NDVI the green-up date.

Six tabs, one question each: Overview (the verdict), Water (water needed vs received), Heat (hot, dry days at flowering), Sowing (the date with the best harvest in the worst one-in-five year, by CVaR - and what sowing late costs, in tenge), Replay (any season 1984-2026, played day by day), Confidence (the score’s uncertainty band, its reasons, and the back-test).

Does it hold up - three independent checks. Nationally, the score tracks 33 years of real wheat yield (ρ = -0.63, in-sample and leave-one-out, p < 0.001). Per district, all nine points are now scored against their own official 2012-2020 harvest (Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan): three track significantly (strongest ρ = -0.88), the pooled signal is ρ = -0.42, and where a point sits in humid forest-steppe - where drought isn’t the driver - it says “no skill” instead of pretending. Because the regional series is only nine years, below our ten-year bar, the national check stays the headline.

Impact. A rainfed farmer in Akmola or Kostanay gets a field-level warning weeks before harvest and a sowing date chosen for the bad year - free, no login, no sensors, in Russian or English. Kazakhstan feeds much of Central Asia, so one drought becomes a regional price shock. Open data plus textbook physics means the method transfers to any rainfed grain belt on Earth.

Creativity. The new step is turning a textbook water balance into a decision a farmer reads in two seconds - and a time machine to check the model against real history before trusting it. Every number traces to a cited equation and a dated file.

Honesty over coverage. Only spring wheat passes a harvest back-test; the other seven crops are marked “experimental,” and for sorghum and millet the model says “does not ripen here” rather than invent a date. The three calibrated fields and six districts load instantly; any other point fetches NASA data live. The model layer has no network and no clock, so every result is reproducible.

Tools. TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind 4, MapLibre GL JS; ~1,400 Vitest tests with FAO-56 worked examples as known answers; Vercel, no backend, no database (field state lives in the URL). Data: NASA POWER, SMAP SPL4SMGP, MODIS MOD13Q1, SRTM, ESA WorldCover, SoilGrids 2.0, FAOSTAT, Bureau of National Statistics KZ.

Limitations. (1) Only spring wheat passes a harvest back-test (ρ = -0.63, 1992-2024); barley is weak (ρ = -0.39), canola not significant (p ≈ 0.18), the other five crops have no yield data.

(2) District validation now runs on official 2012-2020 yields, but nine years is below our ten-year bar, so points fall back to national for the headline - a data limit, not a code gap; three districts are already significant.

(3) Harvest checks use published years only, so 2025-2026 can’t be validated yet.

(4) SMAP starts in 2015; earlier seasons (including 2012) start from a snowmelt estimate or full profile.
